data: The brightest and (after Miranda) youngest-looking surface in the Uranian system — Voyager 2 imagery shows broad rift valleys and what may be flow features hinting at past or present cryovolcanic activity. Tidal heating from a 2:1 orbital resonance with Umbriel that existed in the deep past could have melted the interior; whether any liquid water remains today is unknown. Like the other Uranian major moons, only its southern hemisphere has been imaged at close range.

Water-ice crust + silicate / carbonaceous rock interior; surface the brightest of Uranus's major moons, with relatively few craters — interpreted as evidence of cryovolcanic resurfacing within the last ~1 Gyr.
Ariel orbits at 190,900 km from Uranus — second-innermost of the major moons. Like all Uranian moons, its orbit shares the planet's 97° axial tilt.
Half the longest diameter of the orbit ellipse — and the single number that sets the orbital period.
